headline: UK economy grows 0.1% in August, beating forecasts of a contraction

terms.meaning: The total value of goods and services produced in a country; the main measure of the size of the economy.
The gap between what the government plans to borrow and the limit its own rules allow.

levels.headline: UK economy grows 0.1% in August, beating forecasts of a contraction
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.1% in August, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), beating forecasts that output would shrink. It followed a 0.4% rise in July, so growth slowed from one month to the next.
On an annual basis GDP was 2.1% higher than a year earlier, ahead of the 1.7% economists expected. The ONS said this was the strongest year-on-year reading since August 2022.
The picture is mixed. Consumer spending fell during the month, and analysts expect inflation to rise towards the end of the year as higher oil and gas prices reach household bills. Nearly three-quarters of businesses (72%) reported some concern about energy prices in late September.
The figures matter for the Budget on 28 October, Chancellor John Healey's first. Slower growth tends to reduce tax revenue and so narrows the fiscal headroom he has to work with.
levels.why: Growth beat expectations, but the Chancellor still faces a tight Budget on 28 October.

levels.headline: UK economy edges up 0.1% in August, beating expectations of a fall
levels.body:
UK gross domestic product rose 0.1% in August, the ONS said, confounding forecasts of a contraction. July's increase had been a stronger 0.4%, so the monthly pace cooled.
Over twelve months GDP grew 2.1%, comfortably above the 1.7% economists predicted and the highest annual rate since August 2022.
The detail is less cheerful. Household spending fell, and analysts expect inflation to climb later this year as higher oil and gas prices feed through to energy bills. A survey found 72% of businesses were at least somewhat worried about energy costs in late September.
Chancellor John Healey delivers his first Budget on 28 October. A slowing economy tends to bring in less tax, which squeezes the fiscal headroom, the margin by which he can spend more or cut taxes while still meeting the government's own borrowing rules.
levels.why: Weaker growth gives the Chancellor less room for manoeuvre in his Budget.

levels.headline: UK economy grows slightly in August, more than expected
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.1% in August, the Office for National Statistics reported. Economists had expected it to shrink slightly, so the result was better than predicted. In July, the economy had grown by 0.4%.
Compared with a year earlier, the economy was 2.1% bigger. That was higher than the 1.7% forecast and the best annual figure since August 2022.
However, people spent less in the shops and elsewhere, and experts think prices will start to rise faster again as oil and gas get more expensive. Most businesses, 72% in one survey, say they are worried about energy prices.
This matters because the Chancellor, John Healey, will set out his first Budget on 28 October. When growth is weak, the government collects less tax, leaving less room to spend or cut taxes.
levels.why: The figures will shape how much the Chancellor can offer in his Budget.

levels.headline: UK economy grew a little in August, beating forecasts
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.1% in August, official figures show. Experts had thought it would shrink, so this was a pleasant surprise. The month before, growth had been 0.4%.
Over the past year the economy has grown by 2.1%. That is better than the 1.7% experts predicted, and it is the best yearly figure for more than four years.
But there are worries. People spent less money last month, and prices are expected to rise faster by the end of the year because oil and gas cost more. In a recent survey, nearly three in four firms said they were concerned about energy bills.
The Chancellor, John Healey, will deliver his first Budget on 28 October. Slower growth means less tax money coming in, which could make his decisions harder.
levels.why: A weaker economy can make it harder for the government to spend or cut taxes.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew slightly in August, which surprised experts
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.1% in August. This was a small rise, but experts had expected a small fall, so it was good news. GDP, the measure of everything the country makes and sells, had risen by 0.4% in July.
Compared with last year, the economy is 2.1% bigger. That is the best yearly growth since August 2022.
There is still some worry. Shoppers spent less, and energy costs are going up, which is likely to push prices higher later this year. Many businesses told researchers they are anxious about their gas and electricity bills.
The Chancellor, John Healey, will announce his Budget on 28 October. The Budget is when the government says how it will raise and spend money. With slower growth, it has less spare money, which experts call fiscal headroom.
levels.why: Growth affects how much money the government has to spend on public services.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew a bit in August
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.1% in August. That is a very small rise. But experts thought the economy would shrink, so many people were pleased. The economy is often measured by GDP, which means the total value of all the things made and services sold in the country.
Over the last year, the economy has grown by 2.1%. This is the best year-on-year result since 2022.
However, people spent less money last month. Oil and gas are getting more expensive too. That means prices in shops and energy bills may go up again soon. Lots of businesses say this worries them.
On 28 October the Chancellor, John Healey, will explain how the government plans to use money. If the economy grows slowly, the government gets less tax and has less to spend.
levels.why: Slow growth can mean less money for public services or higher taxes.

levels.headline: Britain's economy grew a tiny bit last month
levels.body:
Britain's economy grew a tiny bit in August. It went up by 0.1%. Experts had guessed it would go down, so this was a nice surprise. The economy means all the things people make, buy and sell in a country.
Looking back over a whole year, the economy is 2.1% bigger. That is the best result for over four years.
But people bought less in August. Oil and gas also cost more now. That can make bills and prices rise. Many businesses are worried about this.
Soon the Chancellor will share a plan called the Budget. He is the person in charge of the country's money. His name is John Healey. When the economy grows slowly, the government collects less tax. Then it has less money to spend on things like hospitals and schools.
levels.why: It helps decide whether the government can pay for services without raising taxes.

levels.headline: Britain made and sold a bit more last month than expected
levels.body:
Last month, Britain made and sold a little more than the month before. The amount went up by 0.1%. We call this the economy. It means all the work people do and all the things they buy and sell.
Grown-ups who study money had thought the economy would get a little smaller. So this news was better than they hoped. Over the whole year, the economy has grown by 2.1%.
But people bought fewer things in shops last month. And oil and gas are getting dearer, so bills might go up. Lots of shops and firms feel nervous about that.
The person who looks after the country's money is called the Chancellor. He will share a big plan on 28 October. If the country earns less, there is less to share out.
levels.why: It affects how much money there is for schools, hospitals and your family's bills.

levels.headline: Britain's money-making grew a little bit last month
levels.body:
Last month, Britain's economy grew by a tiny amount, just 0.1%. The economy is all the things that people and businesses make, sell and buy. Grown-ups who study money had thought it would shrink, so this was a happy surprise.
If you look at a whole year, Britain is making and selling 2.1% more than it did before. That has not happened this quickly for over four years.
But shoppers spent less last month. Oil and gas also cost more, which can make heating bills and food go up in price. Many businesses are worried about it.
Soon, the Chancellor, who is in charge of the country's money, will share his plan. It is called the Budget. When the economy is slow, the government gets less tax, so it has less money to spend.
levels.why: It affects how much money the government has for schools, hospitals and bills.

levels.headline: Britain's pocket money pot grew a tiny bit
levels.body:
Think of Britain as a big family with a pot of money. Everyone earns some money by working and spends some money in shops. Last month, the pot grew just a tiny bit. It was only a very small growth, but the grown-ups had expected it to shrink.
Over one whole year, the pot has grown by a bit more. That is good news.
But there is a worry. Oil and gas, which keep our homes warm, are costing more. That is like your favourite sweets going up in price. Then people cannot buy as much with the same pocket money.
Soon, the person in charge of the country's money, called the Chancellor, will make a plan for how to share the pot. A smaller pot means harder choices.
levels.why: When the money pot is small, it is harder to pay for things like schools.

headline: S&P 500 falls 1.1% as Nasdaq slides 2% on AI sell-off and rising oil

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 large US companies, widely used as a gauge of the US stock market.
A stock index dominated by technology companies.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, an index of 30 large US companies.

levels.headline: S&P 500 falls 1.1% as Nasdaq slides 2% on AI sell-off and rising oil
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on Friday 16 October, the last completed session, falling 1.09% to 7,659.44. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.14% to 26,140.03, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to end at 52,002.41.
Technology and artificial intelligence shares led the decline as investors rotated away from the sector. A rise in oil prices also weighed on sentiment, and wholesale inflation this week recorded its biggest gain since 2022.
Over the week the Nasdaq fell more than 4%, its worst week since June, while the Dow gained 0.7%. The S&P 500 now sits roughly 2% below the record close it set earlier this month.
The divergence between the Nasdaq and the Dow shows money moving out of AI-linked growth stocks, even as broader markets held up better. Higher oil prices and inflation fears also raise the chance that interest rates stay high for longer.
levels.why: Falling tech shares and rising oil show investors are worried about inflation and the AI boom.

levels.headline: US stocks fall as tech sell-off deepens, with the Nasdaq down more than 2%
levels.body:
The S&P 500 fell 1.09% on Friday 16 October, the latest completed session, to close at 7,659.44. The Nasdaq Composite slid 2.14% to 26,140.03, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.34%, or 175.28 points, to 52,002.41.
Investors sold technology and AI-related shares and moved money elsewhere, while higher oil prices and a jump in wholesale inflation this week added to the unease.
The Nasdaq lost over 4% across the week, its worst since June, although the Dow actually rose 0.7%. The S&P 500 is about 2% below the record close it reached earlier in October.
In simple terms, many investors are worried that spending on AI may not pay off quickly, and that rising energy costs could keep inflation and interest rates higher for longer, which tends to hurt company valuations.
levels.why: Rising oil and inflation fears are weighing on share prices, which can affect pensions and savings.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends the week lower as tech shares tumble
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed lower on Friday 16 October, the last full trading day, down 1.09% at 7,659.44. The Nasdaq, which is packed with technology firms, fell 2.14% to 26,140.03. The Dow Jones, made up of 30 big US companies, slipped 0.34% to 52,002.41.
Shares in technology and artificial intelligence companies were sold heavily. Oil prices also rose, and prices paid to producers this week went up by the most since 2022.
For the week, the Nasdaq lost more than 4%, its worst week since June. The Dow rose 0.7%. The S&P 500 is about 2% below the record it set earlier this month.
Investors are moving money out of AI companies and worrying that dearer oil will push up prices, which could keep interest rates high.
levels.why: Moves in US shares affect pension funds and investments held by ordinary savers.

levels.headline: US shares fall on Friday as investors sell technology companies
levels.body:
US shares ended lower on Friday 16 October, the last day markets were open. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big American companies, fell 1.09% to 7,659.44. The Nasdaq, full of tech firms, dropped 2.14% to 26,140.03. The Dow, which follows 30 large companies, lost 0.34% to finish at 52,002.41.
Investors sold many technology and artificial intelligence companies. The price of oil also went up, and prices that businesses pay each other were rising faster than they have since 2022.
Over the whole week, the Nasdaq fell by more than 4%. That is its worst week since June. The Dow actually rose 0.7%.
The S&P 500 is now around 2% below its record high from earlier this month. Many investors fear higher prices could keep borrowing costs up.
levels.why: Share prices show how confident investors are, and they can affect your savings.

levels.headline: US shares fall on Friday as a tech sell-off hits the Nasdaq hardest
levels.body:
US shares fell on Friday 16 October, the last full day of trading. The S&P 500, an index of 500 large American companies, dropped 1.09% to 7,659.44. The Nasdaq Composite, which is heavy with technology firms, fell 2.14% to 26,140.03. The Dow, an index of 30 big companies, lost 0.34% to close at 52,002.41.
Investors sold technology and artificial intelligence stocks, partly because they doubt the sector can keep growing so fast. Oil prices rose too, and wholesale prices this week climbed by the most since 2022. That matters because higher costs can keep interest rates high.
The Nasdaq lost more than 4% over the week, its worst since June, while the Dow gained 0.7%.
The S&P 500 is about 2% below its record close from earlier this month.
levels.why: Share prices reflect how investors see inflation, interest rates and the AI boom.

levels.headline: Big US share prices dropped on Friday, led by tech firms
levels.body:
On Friday 16 October, share prices in the United States went down. The S&P 500, a list of 500 big American companies, fell 1.09% to 7,659.44. The Nasdaq, which has lots of technology companies, fell 2.14% to 26,140.03. The Dow, a list of 30 large companies, fell 0.34% to 52,002.41.
People sold shares in technology and artificial intelligence, or AI, companies. They are worried those firms may not make as much money as hoped. Oil also became more expensive, and that can push up prices in shops.
In the whole week, the Nasdaq fell more than 4%. The Dow went up by 0.7%.
The S&P 500 is still only about 2% below its highest ever level, which it reached earlier in October.
levels.why: Falling share prices can make investors nervous and may affect savings and pensions.

levels.headline: American share prices fell on Friday
levels.body:
On Friday, share prices in America went down. A share is a small piece of a company that people can buy. When many people want to sell, the price falls.
One big list, called the S&P 500, fell by about 1%. It follows 500 large American companies. Another list, the Nasdaq, fell by about 2%. It has many technology companies. A third list, the Dow, fell by a smaller amount, about a third of one per cent.
Most of the selling was in technology and AI firms. AI means computers that can do clever tasks. Oil also cost more, and that worried people because it can make everything dearer.
The week was mixed. The Nasdaq had a bad week, but the Dow went up a little.
levels.why: Share prices tell us how safe investors feel about the world and the economy.

levels.headline: American share prices went down on Friday, led by computer firms
levels.body:
On Friday 16 October, share prices in the United States went down. A share is a small part of a company, and an index is a list that shows how a group of shares is doing. The S&P 500, which lists 500 big firms, fell by just over 1%, to 7,659.44. The Nasdaq, full of technology firms, fell by about 2%. The Dow, which lists 30 big firms, fell by about a third of one per cent.
Many people sold shares in AI firms. They are less sure those companies will make as much money as hoped. Oil also became dearer, which can push up prices and keep borrowing costs high.
Over the week, the Nasdaq had its worst run since June. The Dow rose a little.
levels.why: Share prices show whether people feel safe about money, and that can affect savings.

levels.headline: Share prices in America went down on Friday
levels.body:
A share is a tiny piece of a company. People buy and sell shares, and the prices go up and down every day. On Friday, many share prices in America went down.
There are lists that show how shares are doing. One list is the S&P 500, with 500 big companies. It fell by a bit over 1%. Another is the Nasdaq, with many computer and technology companies. It fell by about 2%. The Dow, with 30 big companies, fell by only a little.
Many people sold shares in AI companies, which make smart computer programs. They were worried these firms might not earn as much money as people hoped. Oil also became dearer, which can push up prices for lots of things.
Over the whole week, the Nasdaq did badly but the Dow did a little better.
levels.why: It shows whether people feel safe about money, which can change prices and jobs.

levels.headline: Shares are like sweets in a shop, and many got cheaper on Friday
levels.body:
Imagine a school swap shop where children trade little pieces of famous companies. Each piece is called a share. If lots of children want a piece, its price goes up. If lots want to get rid of it, the price goes down.
On Friday in America, many children wanted to get rid of shares in computer and AI companies. So the prices went down. The list that follows 500 big companies went down by a little bit more than one in a hundred. The list full of computer companies went down by about two in a hundred.
Oil also got more expensive, and that made some people worry that everything might cost more.
The week was up and down, but grown-ups are still watching carefully.
levels.why: It shows when people feel worried about money, which can affect lots of families.

headline: Burnham announces matched £10 million for two Scottish defence colleges and a summit with first ministers

terms.meaning: The transfer of powers from the UK government to Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland or local areas.
A forum bringing UK ministers together with the leaders of the devolved governments to discuss the economy.

levels.headline: Burnham announces matched £10 million for two Scottish defence colleges and a summit with first ministers
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham used a speech in Scotland on 16 October to say the Scottish government has agreed to match the UK government's £10 million to create two defence technical excellence colleges, one in the east and one in the west.
He linked the colleges to jobs in a defence sector that already supports 12,000 jobs in Scotland.
Burnham also said the National Economic Council, a body revived by his government, will meet in about two weeks with the First Ministers of Scotland and Wales and the First Minister and Deputy First Minister of Northern Ireland. It will be the first such meeting since he became Prime Minister. He said it would be a chance to put his devolution offer on the table and work out a plan together, including how research and innovation money is decided.
The announcement shows a more cooperative approach between Westminster and the devolved governments.
levels.why: It shows how the UK and Scottish governments are working together on jobs, skills and devolution.

levels.headline: PM says Scotland will match UK funding for two defence colleges
levels.body:
Speaking in Scotland on 16 October, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the Scottish government has agreed to match the UK's £10 million to set up two defence technical excellence colleges, one in the east of the country and one in the west.
He said defence already supports 12,000 jobs in Scotland, and the colleges are meant to train people for skilled work in the sector.
He also announced that the National Economic Council will meet in around two weeks with the leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. He described it as an opportunity to put the devolution offer on the table and agree a plan, including how money for research and innovation is allocated.
The meeting will be the first of its kind since Burnham took office, so it will be watched for signs of how far he will go in sharing power.
levels.why: The meeting tests how much power the new Prime Minister is willing to share.

levels.headline: Scotland to match UK money for two new defence colleges
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a speech in Scotland on 16 October that the Scottish government will match £10 million from the UK government. The money will create two defence technical excellence colleges, one in the east and one in the west of Scotland.
Burnham said the defence industry already supports 12,000 jobs in Scotland. The colleges are aimed at giving people the skills those jobs need.
He also said that in about two weeks the National Economic Council will meet the leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. This is the first time it will do so since he became Prime Minister. He said they would talk about handing more decisions to local and national governments and about how money for research and new ideas is shared out.
levels.why: The plan could create skilled jobs and show whether the UK's governments can cooperate.

levels.headline: PM says Scotland will join the UK in paying for two defence colleges
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited Scotland on 16 October. He said the Scottish government has agreed to put in £10 million, the same as the UK government, to build two colleges. They will teach technical skills for the defence industry. One will be in the east of Scotland and one in the west.
The defence industry already provides 12,000 jobs in Scotland, and the colleges are meant to help people train for them.
Burnham also said a group called the National Economic Council will meet in about two weeks. It brings together the UK government and the leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. They will discuss devolution, which means giving more power to those nations, and how money for research should be shared.
levels.why: It shows how governments across the UK might share money, power and jobs.

levels.headline: Scotland and the UK will each put £10 million into two defence colleges
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, gave a speech in Scotland on 16 October. He said the Scottish government and the UK government will each pay £10 million to set up two new colleges. They will teach practical skills for jobs in defence, such as working with technology. There will be one college in the east of Scotland and one in the west.
About 12,000 jobs in Scotland already depend on the defence industry.
He also said that in about two weeks, leaders from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will meet UK ministers in a group called the National Economic Council. They will talk about devolution, which means local leaders making more of their own decisions, and about how money for new research gets shared fairly.
levels.why: Training more people could mean more skilled jobs, and fair sharing of money matters to every nation.

levels.headline: Scotland and the UK will share the cost of two defence colleges
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, was in Scotland on 16 October. He said the Scottish government has agreed to pay £10 million towards two new colleges, matching what the UK government is paying. The colleges will train people for jobs in defence, which means work that helps protect the country. One will be in the east and one in the west.
Defence already provides 12,000 jobs in Scotland, so training could help more people find skilled work.
Burnham also said that in about two weeks, leaders from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will meet UK ministers. They will talk about devolution, which means local governments having more say, and about how money for research is shared out.
levels.why: It shows whether the UK's governments can work together on jobs and money.

levels.headline: Two new defence colleges planned for Scotland
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, spoke in Scotland on 16 October. He said two new colleges will be built there. They will teach people the skills needed for jobs in defence. That means work for the armed forces and the companies that supply them. One college will be in the east and one in the west.
The UK government and the Scottish government will each pay £10 million.
About 12,000 people in Scotland already work in defence jobs.
The Prime Minister also said that in about two weeks, leaders from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will meet UK ministers. They will talk about how decisions and money are shared between the nations of the UK. Sharing power like this is called devolution.
levels.why: It could give people new training and jobs, and show how the UK's nations work together.

levels.headline: The UK and Scottish governments will each pay for two new colleges
levels.body:
The Prime Minister is the person who leads the UK government. His name is Andy Burnham. On 16 October he went to Scotland and gave a speech.
He said two new colleges will open there to teach people skills for working in defence. Defence means protecting the country. The UK government and the Scottish government will each give £10 million to pay for them. One college will be in the east of Scotland and one in the west.
More than 12,000 people in Scotland already work in defence.
He also said that soon the leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will meet UK ministers to talk about money and who makes which decisions. Sharing out power like this is called devolution.
levels.why: It means new training places and shows how leaders of different nations can share the work.

levels.headline: Two new colleges are coming to Scotland
levels.body:
The Prime Minister leads the country. He is called Andy Burnham. This week he visited Scotland to talk about two new colleges.
These colleges will teach grown-ups and young people how to do special jobs. The jobs help to protect the country. Some people call this work defence. One college will be in the east of Scotland. The other will be in the west.
The college plan will cost money. The UK government will pay £10 million. The Scottish government will pay the same amount.
The Prime Minister said he will also meet the leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland soon. They will talk together about how to share money and who makes decisions in each place.
levels.why: Colleges give people skills for work, and leaders talking together can help everyone.

levels.headline: Two governments are sharing the cost of new colleges, like friends sharing a bill
levels.body:
Imagine two friends who want to build a clubhouse. One friend has some money. The other friend has the same amount. If they put it together, they can build something good.
That is what happened in Scotland. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said the UK government and the Scottish government will each give £10 million. They will use it to build two new colleges. A college is a place where people learn how to do a job well. These ones will teach skills for protecting the country.
One will be in the east of Scotland. One will be in the west.
Soon the grown-up leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will meet to talk about sharing things fairly.
levels.why: When leaders share the costs and listen to each other, more people can learn new things.

headline: Healey's first Budget on 28 October faces high borrowing costs and slowing growth

terms.meaning: Bonds issued by the UK government to borrow money.
The return an investor gets on a bond; a higher yield means the government pays more to borrow.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget on 28 October faces high borrowing costs and slowing growth
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver his first Budget on 28 October, the first under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, with the government's room for manoeuvre under pressure.
The yield on the 10-year gilt, the interest the government pays to borrow for a decade, was around 5.3% in mid-October. It reached 5.44% earlier in the autumn, the highest since July 2007. Higher borrowing costs eat into fiscal headroom, the margin left under the government's own borrowing rules, and raise expectations of tax rises.
The slowdown in monthly growth to 0.1% in August adds to the strain. Healey has said he wants a buffer against uncertainty, and ministers have yet to set out the full mix of savings or taxes needed, including to fund defence spending.
A former Bank of England chief economist has warned Britain is on thin ice and must act to appease financial markets.
levels.why: The Budget will decide taxes and spending, so it affects households and businesses.

levels.headline: Chancellor faces a squeeze on 28 October as gilt yields stay near multi-year highs
levels.body:
John Healey will present his first Budget as Chancellor on 28 October, the first of Andy Burnham's government. He faces rising debt interest costs and weaker growth.
The 10-year gilt yield was about 5.3% in mid-October. Earlier this autumn it hit 5.44%, the highest since July 2007. When yields rise, the cost of government borrowing rises with them, which shrinks the fiscal headroom, the gap between planned borrowing and the limit set by the government's rules.
Growth of just 0.1% in August adds pressure. Healey has spoken of a buffer against uncertainty, but the mix of savings and tax rises needed, including to fund defence, has not been spelled out.
A former Bank of England chief economist has said Britain is on thin ice and must reassure markets.
levels.why: High borrowing costs can lead to higher taxes or less spending on public services.

levels.headline: Chancellor's first Budget comes as borrowing costs stay high
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver his first Budget on 28 October. It is the first Budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
The government pays interest when it borrows, and that interest rate has been high. The yield on 10-year gilts, which are government bonds, was around 5.3% in mid-October. Earlier this autumn it hit 5.44%, the highest since 2007. Higher costs leave the government less spare money, known as fiscal headroom, under its own rules.
Slow growth makes this harder, as the economy grew just 0.1% in August. Healey wants a buffer against uncertainty, but ministers have not yet said how they will raise money or save it, including to pay for defence.
A former Bank of England economist has warned Britain is on thin ice.
levels.why: The Budget affects tax, spending and the cost of borrowing for everyone.

levels.headline: The Chancellor's Budget is due on 28 October, with money tight
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will set out his first Budget on 28 October. It is the first since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister.
The government borrows money by selling bonds called gilts. It has to pay interest on them, and that interest has become expensive. The 10-year rate was about 5.3% in mid-October, and it went as high as 5.44% earlier this autumn, the highest since 2007. That leaves less spare money, called headroom, within the rules the government has set itself.
Economic growth is also slowing, which brings in less tax. Healey says he wants a safety buffer. But he has not yet explained how much tax or saving may be needed, including for defence.
One former Bank of England expert says Britain is on thin ice.
levels.why: It may decide whether taxes rise or public spending is held back.

levels.headline: The Chancellor must balance the books on 28 October, and it will not be easy
levels.body:
On 28 October the Chancellor, John Healey, will announce his first Budget. A Budget is when the government says how it will raise and spend money.
The government often borrows by selling gilts, which are promises to pay back money with interest. Right now that interest is high. For a 10-year gilt it was about 5.3% in mid-October, and earlier it reached 5.44%, the highest since 2007. High costs mean less spare money for the government.
The economy is also growing slowly, so less tax comes in. Healey wants a safety cushion in case things go wrong. But it is not yet clear whether he will raise taxes or cut spending, and defence will also need money.
levels.why: The choices made could change taxes, public services and prices for ordinary families.

levels.headline: The Chancellor's big money plan is coming, and the country is short of cash
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, will share his Budget on 28 October. A Budget is the government's plan for how to collect and spend money.
The government borrows money, a bit like a loan. When it does, it must pay extra, called interest. This interest has become more expensive. It was about 5.3% in mid-October. Earlier it was 5.44%, which was the highest for almost 20 years. That leaves less spare money.
The economy is also growing slowly, so the government gets less money from taxes. The Chancellor says he wants a safety cushion in case something goes wrong. People do not yet know if he will raise taxes or spend less. The country also needs money for defence.
levels.why: It decides how much tax people pay and how much the government can spend.

levels.headline: The Chancellor's money plan will be hard this year
levels.body:
The Chancellor looks after the country's money. His name is John Healey. On 28 October he will share his plan for the year, called the Budget.
The government sometimes has to borrow money. It must pay back a bit extra, called interest. That extra is now expensive. It is about as high as it has been for almost 20 years. This means the government has less money left over.
The country is also growing slowly. When that happens, the government collects less tax.
The Chancellor wants some spare money for emergencies. He has not said yet if he will make people pay more tax or spend less on things. The country also needs to pay for defence.
levels.why: Taxes and spending touch schools, hospitals and what people pay each month.

levels.headline: The government is short of money before its big plan
levels.body:
The government is like a very big family that needs to pay for lots of things. It pays for schools, hospitals and the army. The money mostly comes from taxes, which people and businesses pay.
The person in charge is the Chancellor, John Healey. On 28 October he will share his plan for the money. It is called the Budget.
Things are tricky. The government has borrowed money, and it has to pay extra to give it back. That extra has become costly. The country is also not growing very quickly, so less tax is coming in.
He has not yet said whether people will pay more tax or whether the government will spend less.
levels.why: It shows how a country has to make choices when there is not enough money.

levels.headline: The country's pocket money plan is coming, but there is not much to spare
levels.body:
Imagine a family has a jar of money. The grown-ups use it to pay for food, school things and holidays. Sometimes they have to borrow money from a friend. When they pay it back, they have to give a little extra.
Right now, the extra costs are big, so there is less money left in the jar.
The person who looks after the country's money is the Chancellor. He is called John Healey. On 28 October he will say how the country will earn money and how it will spend it. This is called the Budget.
He has not said if people will pay more or if the country will spend less. Everyone is waiting to find out.
levels.why: It matters because the country's choices about money touch every family.

levels.headline: A Budget is like a big plan for the family's money
levels.body:
Every family has to think about money. How much comes in? How much goes out? And what should we save for a rainy day?
A country must think the same way. The Chancellor, John Healey, will share the country's money plan on 28 October. It is called the Budget.
This time it is hard. The country has borrowed money and now the extra it must pay back has become big. That means there is less money left in the pot. The country is also growing very slowly, so not as much money is coming in.
Nobody knows yet what the plan will say. People will be watching to see if they must pay more or if the country will buy less.
levels.why: A fair money plan helps the country pay for things like schools and hospitals.

headline: UK inflation figures due on 21 October, with the Bank of England under pressure to raise rates

terms.meaning: The rate at which prices rise over time.
The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences mortgage, savings and loan rates.
The Bank of England group of nine that votes on interest rates.

levels.headline: UK inflation figures due on 21 October, with the Bank of England under pressure to raise rates
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics will publish September's inflation figure on 21 October. Forecasts point to 3.4%, up from 3.1% in August, which was the first reading above 3% since March. Motor fuel costs were the main driver of the August rise.
The Bank of England has held Bank Rate at 3.75% since December 2025. At its September meeting its Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to hold, with the three dissenters wanting a rise to 4%. The Committee blamed the prolonged Middle East conflict for pushing up energy prices and said inflation risks lean to the upside.
Markets widely expect a rise of at least 0.25 percentage points at the November meeting, and the Bank has said it is ready to tighten policy if needed.
Higher oil and gas prices are expected to feed through to household bills towards the end of the year.
levels.why: Higher inflation and a possible rate rise would affect mortgages, savings and living costs.

levels.headline: UK inflation expected to rise again as the Bank of England weighs a rate hike
levels.body:
UK inflation for September is due from the ONS on 21 October, with forecasters expecting 3.4% after 3.1% in August. August was the first time inflation had topped 3% since March, driven mainly by motor fuel costs.
Bank Rate has stood at 3.75% since December 2025. In September the Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to hold, with three members preferring a rise to 4%. It said the long Middle East conflict is pushing up energy prices and that risks to inflation remain on the upside.
Markets expect an increase of at least a quarter of a percentage point in November, and the Bank says it will tighten if necessary.
Economists expect higher oil and gas prices to reach household bills later this year.
levels.why: Rising prices and higher interest rates both squeeze household budgets.

levels.headline: Inflation is expected to rise again, and interest rates could follow
levels.body:
The next UK inflation figure, for September, comes out on 21 October. Experts expect 3.4%, up from 3.1% in August, when inflation went above 3% for the first time since March. Petrol and diesel prices were the main reason.
The Bank of England has kept its main interest rate at 3.75% since December 2025. In September, six of its nine rate-setters voted to keep it there, but three wanted to raise it to 4%. They said the war in the Middle East is pushing up energy prices.
Many investors now expect the Bank to raise rates by at least 0.25 percentage points in November. The Bank says it is ready to act if prices keep rising.
levels.why: Higher rates can make mortgages and loans more expensive, though they help savers.

levels.headline: Prices are expected to keep rising faster, which may push up interest rates
levels.body:
Inflation is how fast prices rise. On 21 October the government will publish the figure for September. Experts expect 3.4%, compared with 3.1% in August. August was the first month since March that it went above 3%, mostly because fuel cost more.
The Bank of England sets the main interest rate, which has been 3.75% since December 2025. In September, three of its nine decision makers wanted to raise it to 4%, but six voted to leave it. The Bank said the conflict in the Middle East is making energy dearer.
Investors now think the rate may rise in November. The Bank says it is ready to act if it needs to, to stop prices rising too quickly.
levels.why: Interest rates affect what people pay on mortgages and earn on savings.

levels.headline: Prices may rise faster, and borrowing could get dearer
levels.body:
Inflation means prices going up over time. Last month, UK prices were 3.1% higher than a year before. Experts think the next figure, out on 21 October, will be higher, at 3.4%. Petrol and diesel costing more was the main reason.
The Bank of England is in charge of the main interest rate. This is the price of borrowing money, and it affects mortgages and savings. It has been 3.75% since December 2025. In September, three of nine members wanted it raised to 4%, but most wanted to wait.
The Bank blames the war in the Middle East, which is making oil and gas dearer. Many investors expect the Bank to raise the rate in November, and the Bank says it is ready to do so.
levels.why: It could change the cost of mortgages and the value of savings.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, so interest rates could go up
levels.body:
Inflation is the speed at which prices rise. In August, UK prices were 3.1% higher than a year before, and experts think the figure published on 21 October will be 3.4%. A big reason is that petrol and diesel have become more expensive.
The Bank of England controls the main interest rate, which is the cost of borrowing money. It has been 3.75% since December 2025. In September, three of the nine members who vote wanted to raise it to 4%, but six voted to keep it where it was.
The Bank says the conflict in the Middle East is pushing up energy prices. Many investors expect a rise in November. If that happens, mortgages and loans could cost more, while savings might earn a little more.
levels.why: Both prices and interest rates change how far a family's money goes.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster, and the rules for borrowing money might change
levels.body:
When prices go up each year, we call it inflation. In August, prices were 3.1% higher than a year earlier. People expect the next number, due on 21 October, to be 3.4%. Fuel for cars got dearer, and that is a big reason.
The Bank of England is a special bank that helps look after the country's money. It sets a rate that decides how costly it is to borrow money. That rate is 3.75%. In September, three of the nine people who decide wanted to raise it. Most voted to keep it the same.
The Bank says fighting in the Middle East makes oil and gas cost more. Many people think the rate will go up in November.
levels.why: If borrowing costs rise, families with mortgages may have to pay more each month.

levels.headline: Shop prices keep climbing, and the Bank may act
levels.body:
Inflation means the cost of things rises over time. Imagine a pack of crisps costs 100p one year, and 103p the next. That is inflation of 3%. In August, prices in the UK rose by 3.1% over the year. People expect the next number, out on 21 October, to be 3.4%.
One big reason is that petrol is dearer. That is because of fighting in the Middle East, which makes oil and gas cost more.
The Bank of England helps keep prices steady. It sets an interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. At the moment it is 3.75%. In September, three of the nine decision makers wanted to make it higher. Many people think it could go up in November.
levels.why: It affects what you pay in shops and what families pay on loans.

levels.headline: Prices at the shops keep going up, a bit like sweets costing more each year
levels.body:
Imagine your favourite sweets cost £1 last year. This year they cost a little more. When lots of things cost more, we call it inflation. In the UK, prices are now 3.1% higher than a year ago. Grown-ups think the next number will be 3.4%.
One reason is that oil, which makes petrol for cars, has become more expensive. There is fighting far away in the Middle East, and it makes oil harder to get.
There is a bank, the Bank of England, which helps keep prices steady. It has a number called the interest rate. This is like a fee for borrowing money. At the moment it is 3.75%. The bank might make it bigger soon, to slow prices down.
levels.why: It can change how far your family's money goes at the shops.

levels.headline: The Bank of England might change a number that affects everyone's money
levels.body:
Think about a school tuck shop. If prices go up a little each week, your pocket money buys less. This is called inflation. Right now, prices in the UK are going up faster than the grown-ups want.
There is a very important bank called the Bank of England. Its job is to try to stop prices rising too fast. It has a special number, called the interest rate. If you borrow money from a bank, you pay a little extra, and the interest rate decides how much. It is now 3.75%.
Some people at the bank want to make this number bigger, because oil costs more. That could make borrowing dearer. We will find out in a few weeks.
levels.why: It helps stop prices rising too fast, so families can plan their money.

headline: Iran steps up attacks on shipping near Hormuz as talks with Washington stall

terms.meaning: A narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which a large share of the world's oil ships pass.
When a country uses its navy to stop ships entering or leaving another country's ports.

levels.headline: Iran steps up attacks on shipping near Hormuz as talks with Washington stall
levels.body:
At least nine commercial ships have come under attack near the Strait of Hormuz since Sunday, as Iran tries to choke off oil exports through the strait. US Central Command said Iran sank the container ship GFS Pride on Wednesday, and Iran's armed forces also struck two tankers outside the strait within 24 hours, one off Qatar and one off Fujairah.
Iran says it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month. President Trump reimposed the blockade on 14 July after earlier attacks on tankers.
Diplomacy appears stalled: Washington rejected Iran's proposal to reopen Hormuz in return for lifting the blockade. The US is reportedly sending a third aircraft carrier group to the region, and Trump is said to be weighing resumed bombing of Iran after the midterm elections.
levels.why: The conflict threatens a key oil route, so it affects fuel prices and inflation around the world.

levels.headline: Attacks on ships near Hormuz intensify and diplomacy stalls
levels.body:
At least nine commercial vessels have been attacked near the Strait of Hormuz since Sunday. US Central Command said Iran sank the container ship GFS Pride on Wednesday. Iran also hit two tankers outside the strait in 24 hours, one off Qatar and one off Fujairah.
Iran says it is hitting back at the US blockade of its ports and at new sanctions. Donald Trump restored the blockade on 14 July after earlier tanker attacks.
Talks look stuck. The US turned down an Iranian offer to reopen Hormuz if the blockade were lifted. A third US aircraft carrier group is reportedly heading to the Middle East, and Trump is said to be considering bombing Iran again after the midterm elections.
levels.why: Disruption to shipping in the Gulf pushes up oil prices and the cost of living.

levels.headline: Iran attacks more ships as the US blockade continues
levels.body:
At least nine ships have been attacked near the Strait of Hormuz since Sunday, as Iran tries to stop oil leaving the region. The US military said Iran sank the container ship GFS Pride on Wednesday. Iran also struck two oil tankers outside the strait, one near Qatar and one near Fujairah.
Iran says it is attacking because the United States is blocking its ports with its navy and has added tougher sanctions. President Trump brought the blockade back on 14 July.
Talks have not made progress. The US said no to an Iranian offer to reopen the strait if the blockade ended. Reports say a third American aircraft carrier group is heading to the region, and Trump may restart bombing after the midterm elections.
levels.why: A key shipping route is under threat, which can raise prices for fuel and goods.

levels.headline: Iran hits more ships near a key oil route, and peace talks are stuck
levels.body:
At least nine ships have been attacked near the Strait of Hormuz since Sunday. This narrow stretch of water is one of the world's most important routes for oil. The US military said Iran sank a container ship called GFS Pride on Wednesday. Iran also hit two tankers outside the strait.
Iran says it is hitting back because the United States is using its navy to stop ships reaching Iranian ports. This is called a blockade. America also added new sanctions, meaning limits on trade. President Trump restarted the blockade on 14 July.
The United States turned down an offer from Iran to reopen the strait if the blockade ended. Reports say another American aircraft carrier is on its way.
levels.why: The fighting could keep fuel and energy prices high for ordinary people.

levels.headline: Ships are being attacked in a key sea route, and leaders cannot agree
levels.body:
Iran and the United States are in a standoff. Since Sunday, at least nine ships have been attacked near the Strait of Hormuz. This is a narrow sea passage that a lot of the world's oil has to pass through. America's military said Iran sank a container ship on Wednesday.
Iran says it is attacking because the American navy is stopping ships from reaching Iran's ports. That is called a blockade. America has also made new rules to limit Iran's trade. President Trump brought the blockade back in July.
Iran offered to reopen the passage if the blockade ended. The United States said no. Another large American warship group is reportedly heading to the area.
levels.why: Attacks on oil ships can make petrol and energy more expensive everywhere.

levels.headline: Iran and the US are in a standoff over a key oil sea route
levels.body:
At least nine ships have been attacked near the Strait of Hormuz since Sunday. This is a narrow stretch of sea where a lot of the world's oil travels. The US military says Iran sank a container ship on Wednesday and hit two oil tankers outside the strait.
Iran says it is attacking because the US Navy is stopping ships reaching Iranian ports, which is called a blockade, and because the US added tougher sanctions, meaning limits on trade. President Trump restarted the blockade in July.
Iran offered to reopen the strait if the blockade ended, but the United States said no. Reports say a third American aircraft carrier group is heading to the region, and Trump may restart bombing after the US midterm elections.
levels.why: A standoff here can raise fuel prices and affect the cost of living worldwide.

levels.headline: Ships are being attacked at sea, and two countries cannot agree
levels.body:
There is a dangerous standoff between Iran and the United States. A narrow sea passage called the Strait of Hormuz is where many oil ships travel. Since Sunday, at least nine ships have been attacked there. The American military says Iran sank a big cargo ship.
Iran says it is attacking because American warships are blocking its ports. That means they stop ships from going in or out. This is called a blockade. The United States has also stopped many countries from trading with Iran.
Iran said it would open the passage again if the blockade ended. The United States said no. Reports say another group of American warships is on its way. Leaders have not found a way to agree.
levels.why: When an oil route is unsafe, fuel can cost more for everyone.

levels.headline: Two countries are in a fight about ships and ports
levels.body:
Iran and the United States are not getting along. There is a narrow sea passage near Iran. Lots of ships carrying oil sail through it. Since Sunday, at least nine ships there have been attacked. One big cargo ship sank.
The United States says Iran did it. Iran says it is reacting because American warships are stopping ships from getting to Iran's ports. This is called a blockade. It is like blocking a road so that nobody can drive in or out.
Iran said it would stop if the blockade ended. The United States said no. Now another group of American warships may be on its way. The leaders have not made peace yet.
levels.why: If ships cannot sail safely, oil and other goods can become more costly.

levels.headline: Two countries are stuck in a dangerous argument at sea
levels.body:
Imagine two groups arguing over a road. One group stands in the road so the other cannot get through. The other group then starts knocking over things that belong to everyone.
This is a bit like what is happening at sea near Iran. A narrow sea passage is used by lots of ships carrying oil. Iran is attacking some of those ships. Iran says this is because American warships are stopping ships from reaching its ports.
The United States said no when Iran offered to open the passage if the ships left. Another group of warships may be on its way.
Grown-ups are worried. If oil ships cannot sail safely, petrol could cost more everywhere.
levels.why: A calm solution would keep ships safe and help keep prices steady.

levels.headline: Two countries are fighting over a sea road
levels.body:
Think of the sea as a road for ships. In one place near Iran, the road is very narrow. Lots of ships carrying oil use it. Oil is what makes petrol for cars and helps make electricity.
Recently, ships there have been attacked. Iran is doing some of the attacking. It says it is because America's navy is stopping ships from going to Iran's ports.
Iran said it would stop if America moved away. America said no. Now more American warships may be coming.
The leaders are not talking in a friendly way. That is why many grown-ups are worried. If the sea road is not safe, oil can become more expensive for everyone.
levels.why: We need safe roads at sea so that everyone can get the things they need.

headline: Brent crude touches $110 for the first time since May as Iran escalates Hormuz attacks

terms.meaning: The international benchmark price for crude oil, quoted in US dollars per barrel.
The standard measure for oil, about 159 litres.
The International Energy Agency, which advises major economies on energy and coordinates emergency oil stock releases.

levels.headline: Brent crude touches $110 for the first time since May as Iran escalates Hormuz attacks
levels.body:
Brent crude futures touched $110 a barrel on Friday 16 October, the first time since May, before easing to settle at $109.86, a rise of 3.7%. US West Texas Intermediate gained 3.5% to $101.41.
The jump followed a surge in attacks around the Strait of Hormuz over the past ten days, with Iran saying it was stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports. Data from the energy researcher Kpler put Gulf crude shipments at 9.4 million barrels a day in the week to Wednesday, about 70% of the average before the Iran war. Kpler expects a slow, uneven recovery without a comprehensive political deal.
The International Energy Agency has agreed to release the remaining 100 million barrels from a coordinated stockpile release launched in March.
CNBC also linked the move to Ukraine's vow to hit Russian refineries.
levels.why: Dearer oil feeds into petrol, heating and food prices, which is why central banks watch it closely.

levels.headline: Oil jumps to about $110 a barrel as Iran steps up attacks near Hormuz
levels.body:
Brent crude rose 3.7% on Friday 16 October to settle at $109.86 a barrel, after touching $110 for the first time since May. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate rose 3.5% to $101.41.
The rise came after a surge of attacks around the Strait of Hormuz in the last ten days. Iran says it is responding to the US blockade of its ports. Kpler estimates Gulf crude shipments at 9.4 million barrels a day in the week to Wednesday, around 70% of the level before the Iran war, and expects only a slow and uneven recovery without a political deal.
The International Energy Agency has agreed to release the remaining 100 million barrels from the emergency stocks programme begun in March, which may limit further rises.
levels.why: Higher oil prices push up inflation and strengthen the case for higher interest rates.

levels.headline: Oil price hits $110 a barrel as attacks on ships continue
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, rose 3.7% on Friday 16 October to $109.86 a barrel. It briefly touched $110, the highest since May. The US benchmark, West Texas Intermediate, rose 3.5% to $101.41.
Prices rose because Iran has attacked more ships near the Strait of Hormuz over the past ten days, saying it is reacting to the US blockade of its ports. According to the research firm Kpler, oil leaving the Gulf is about 9.4 million barrels a day, roughly 70% of the amount before the war with Iran.
To help, the International Energy Agency has agreed to release the last 100 million barrels of emergency oil it began releasing in March.
levels.why: Oil prices affect petrol, heating bills and the price of many goods.

levels.headline: Oil climbs to $110 a barrel, its highest since May
levels.body:
The price of oil went up again on Friday 16 October. Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose 3.7% to $109.86 a barrel after briefly touching $110. That is the highest since May. In the United States the main price rose 3.5% to $101.41.
Oil rose because Iran has attacked more ships near the Strait of Hormuz in the last ten days. It says this is because of the US blockade of its ports. A research firm, Kpler, says oil coming out of the Gulf is around 70% of what it was before the war with Iran began.
To calm prices, the International Energy Agency, which advises big economies on energy, will release the last 100 million barrels of emergency oil stocks.
levels.why: Dearer oil usually means dearer petrol and higher bills.

levels.headline: Oil costs more again, near $110 a barrel
levels.body:
The price of oil rose again on Friday 16 October. A barrel of Brent, a main oil price used around the world, cost $109.86 at the end of the day, up 3.7%. At one point it reached $110, the highest since May.
Oil is dearer because ships near the Strait of Hormuz have been attacked. This is a narrow sea route that lots of the world's oil passes through. Iran says it is attacking in response to a US blockade of its ports. Only about 70% of the usual amount of oil is now leaving the Gulf.
An international group that advises countries on energy has agreed to release 100 million barrels of emergency oil to help. A barrel is a standard measure of oil.
levels.why: When oil is dearer, many everyday things become dearer too.

levels.headline: Oil gets more expensive as ships are attacked near Hormuz
levels.body:
On Friday 16 October the price of oil went up. A barrel of Brent oil, which is the price most countries follow, cost $109.86 at the close. That is 3.7% higher than the day before. It is the highest price since May.
Oil is more expensive because ships have been attacked near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route. Iran says it is hitting back at a US blockade of its ports. Because of the attacks, less oil is leaving the Gulf. It is about 70% of the amount before the war.
An energy group that helps many countries has agreed to release 100 million barrels of emergency oil. Oil is used to make petrol, diesel and plastic.
levels.why: When oil costs more, petrol, bills and goods in the shops can all cost more.

levels.headline: Oil costs more because ships in the Gulf are in danger
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. It is used to make petrol, diesel and plastic. On Friday 16 October the price of oil went up to about $110 for a barrel. A barrel is a big container of oil. That is the highest price since May.
Oil is dearer because ships have been attacked near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route. A lot of oil has to travel through it. Iran says it is attacking because the United States is blocking its ports. Less oil is getting out. It is only about 70% of what it was before the war.
A group that advises countries has said it will release 100 million barrels of emergency oil.
levels.why: Oil prices change what we pay for fuel and for lots of things in the shops.

levels.headline: Oil is getting more expensive again
levels.body:
Oil is a liquid from under the ground. People use it to make petrol for cars and plastic. This week, the price went up to about $110 for one barrel, which is a very big container. This is the most it has cost since May.
Why has this happened? Ships carrying oil have been attacked near a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. A lot of the world's oil goes through there. Iran says it is attacking because America is blocking its ports. Now less oil is getting out.
To help, a group of countries has said it will let out 100 million barrels of oil it had saved for emergencies.
levels.why: If oil costs more, petrol and other things can cost more as well.

levels.headline: Oil costs a lot more, and that can make life dearer
levels.body:
Oil is something that comes from under the ground. It makes petrol for cars and gives us plastic. A barrel is a big container of oil. This week, one barrel cost about $110. That is more than at any time since May.
Why is it so dear? Some ships carrying oil were attacked in a small sea passage. Lots of oil has to go through it. Now there is less oil to share, so it costs more. It is like when there are only a few ice creams left and everyone wants one.
Some countries have saved oil for emergencies. They have promised to let out 100 million barrels to help. That might help prices to stop going up.
levels.why: If oil costs more, it can make many things in the shops cost more too.

levels.headline: Oil is like a favourite treat that is running short
levels.body:
Imagine the school tuck shop sells your favourite crisps. Everyone loves them. One day, the lorry that brings the crisps gets held up. There are not enough crisps. So the shop makes them cost more.
Oil is a bit like that. It is a liquid from under the ground that makes petrol for cars. Lots of it travels on ships through a narrow sea passage. Recently, some ships have been attacked there. Less oil is arriving, so it costs more. This week, one barrel, a huge tub of oil, cost about $110.
Grown-ups have a store of spare oil for emergencies. They have promised to share some, to help prices calm down.
levels.why: When oil costs more, lots of other things can cost more, like petrol and food.

headline: EU leaders end Brussels summit without a budget deal and weigh new Ukraine funding

terms.meaning: The EU's executive arm, which proposes laws and manages the budget.
Russian state money frozen in Europe, which some want to lend to Ukraine.

levels.headline: EU leaders end Brussels summit without a budget deal and weigh new Ukraine funding
levels.body:
European Union leaders finished their Brussels summit on 16 October without agreeing the bloc's next seven-year budget, raising doubts about whether a deal can be reached by the end of the year.
They did ask the European Commission for options to cover a new funding gap for Ukraine, on top of the €90 billion loan designed to meet Kyiv's needs for 2026 and 2027. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked for €70 billion of extra support for 2027. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen backed that estimate but said the EU would not carry it alone and that other Western allies should contribute. Zelenskyy also pressed again for immobilised Russian assets to be used, and the idea is being revived as a loan, with Ireland and Denmark open to it.
Migration was contentious: Denmark, Italy and Poland pushed for tougher language, including an indirect reference to Spain's regularisation of about 600,000 undocumented migrants. Talks ran past the expected finish time.
levels.why: Europe's ability to fund Ukraine and agree its own budget affects security and spending across the continent.

levels.headline: EU summit ends with no budget deal as leaders seek ways to fund Ukraine
levels.body:
EU leaders ended a Brussels summit on 16 October with no agreement on the next seven-year EU budget, which casts doubt on whether a deal is possible by the end of the year.
They asked the European Commission for options to fill a new gap in Ukraine's funding, over and above the €90 billion loan covering 2026 and 2027. Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked for €70 billion more for 2027. Ursula von der Leyen supported that figure but said the EU cannot cover all of it and that other allies should help. Zelenskyy again urged the use of frozen Russian assets, which are being revived as a possible loan; Ireland and Denmark were open to it.
On migration, Denmark, Italy and Poland pushed for stronger wording, including an indirect reference to Spain's regularisation of around 600,000 undocumented migrants. Discussions overran.
levels.why: Disagreements over money and migration show how hard it is for the EU's members to act together.

levels.headline: EU leaders fail to agree a budget and look for more money for Ukraine
levels.body:
European Union leaders met in Brussels on 16 October but did not agree the EU's next seven-year budget. That makes it less certain a deal can be done by the end of the year.
They asked the European Commission, the EU's executive body, to come up with options for filling a new gap in Ukraine's funding. This would come on top of a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he needs €70 billion more for 2027. The Commission's president, Ursula von der Leyen, agreed with the figure but said the EU should not pay alone. Zelenskyy also asked again to use frozen Russian assets.
Leaders also argued over migration. Denmark, Italy and Poland wanted tougher wording.
levels.why: The decisions affect Ukraine's defence and how EU countries spend money.

levels.headline: EU leaders leave Brussels without a budget deal
levels.body:
EU leaders ended a summit in Brussels on 16 October without agreeing the bloc's next seven-year budget. People now doubt that a deal can be reached by the end of the year.
They did ask the European Commission to find ways to cover a new shortfall in funding for Ukraine. This is in addition to a €90 billion loan already meant to cover Ukraine's needs in 2026 and 2027. Ukraine's leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, asked for €70 billion of extra help for 2027. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU cannot pay for all of it and wants other allies to help.
The leaders also disagreed about migration, with Denmark, Italy and Poland pushing for tougher language.
levels.why: Without a budget deal, the EU's plans for spending and support for Ukraine stay uncertain.

levels.headline: EU leaders do not agree a budget and argue about migration
levels.body:
EU leaders met in Brussels on 16 October. They did not agree on the EU's budget for the next seven years. Some now worry that a deal may not be ready by the end of this year.
They did ask the European Commission, the group that runs the EU day to day, to find ways to help Ukraine with money. Ukraine already has a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027, but Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says it needs €70 billion more for 2027. The Commission's president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU cannot pay alone.
Leaders also argued about migration, which means people moving to live in other countries. Denmark, Italy and Poland wanted stricter wording.
levels.why: Budget decisions decide how much money the EU can spend on Ukraine and other plans.

levels.headline: European leaders cannot agree on a budget
levels.body:
Leaders from the countries of the European Union met in Brussels on 16 October. They did not agree on how much money the EU will have and how it will spend it over the next seven years. That plan is called a budget.
They also talked about Ukraine, which is at war with Russia. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says his country needs €70 billion more in 2027. The leaders asked the European Commission, which helps run the EU, to find ways to help. The head of the Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU should not pay for all of it.
The leaders also argued about migration, which is about people moving to new countries.
levels.why: These choices decide how Europe helps Ukraine and how its countries share money.

levels.headline: EU leaders meet but cannot agree how to share their money
levels.body:
The European Union is a group of countries in Europe that work together. Their leaders met in Brussels on 16 October. They did not agree on how to share and spend the group's money over the next seven years. This plan is called a budget.
They also talked about helping Ukraine, a country that has been in a war with Russia. Ukraine's leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says it needs €70 billion more next year. The leaders asked a group called the European Commission to find ideas for how to find the money.
They also argued about migration, which means people moving from one country to live in another. Some countries wanted stronger rules.
levels.why: If leaders cannot agree, it is harder for them to help each other and Ukraine.

levels.headline: European leaders did not agree, but they asked for ideas
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe are part of a group called the European Union, or EU. Their leaders met in a city called Brussels. They tried to agree on a plan for money for the next seven years. They could not.
They also talked about Ukraine, a country at war with Russia. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says Ukraine will need a lot more money next year. The leaders asked a team to look for ways to find it. One idea is to borrow some money that belongs to Russia but has been frozen.
They also had a disagreement about migration. That means people moving to live in a different country. Three countries wanted stricter rules.
levels.why: Working together is hard, but leaders have to keep talking to help people.

levels.headline: Leaders of European countries could not agree, like a group choosing a game
levels.body:
Imagine a group of friends trying to pick a game for the whole summer. Everyone wants something different. They talk and talk, but they do not agree. That is a bit like what happened in Brussels.
The leaders of many European countries met to agree on how to share the money of their group, the EU, for the next seven years. They could not agree.
They also talked about helping Ukraine, a country where there is a war. Ukraine's leader said they need lots more money next year. The other leaders asked some helpers to look for ways to find it.
They also disagreed about people moving to live in other countries.
levels.why: Even friends who disagree can keep talking, which is how problems get solved.

levels.headline: Leaders talked for a long time but did not decide
levels.body:
Imagine your class has to choose a trip. Some children want the zoo. Others want the beach. They talk for a very long time and do not agree. In the end, the teacher says, let's think again.
That is a bit like what happened to the leaders of the European Union. They met in a big city called Brussels and talked about how to share their group's money. They did not agree, so they will try again.
They also talked about Ukraine, which needs more help because of a war. They asked clever helpers to look for ideas.
They also disagreed about people moving to new homes in other countries.
levels.why: Leaders have to keep talking until everyone can agree, and that takes time.

headline: US budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12%

terms.meaning: The amount by which a government's spending is greater than the money it collects in a year.
What a government pays in interest on its debt, after deducting interest it receives.

levels.headline: US budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12%
levels.body:
The US federal budget deficit for fiscal 2026 came in at about $1.992 trillion, according to Treasury figures released on 16 October. That is roughly 12% higher than the $1.775 trillion deficit of the previous year and the third-largest on record, behind only 2020 and 2021.
Net interest on the national debt topped $1 trillion, up from $970 billion in fiscal 2025. Social Security was the biggest spending item at nearly $1.7 trillion, followed by Medicare at almost $1.1 trillion. Individual income taxes raised more than $2.8 trillion, but corporate tax receipts fell by about $70 billion, which CNBC links to tax cuts in last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Customs revenue was reduced by refunds after the Supreme Court ruled many tariffs unconstitutional.
It was the 25th straight year of deficits; the last surplus was in 2001.
levels.why: Rising debt interest and 5% Treasury yields make borrowing a growing worry for the US.

levels.headline: US deficit rises to nearly $2 trillion in fiscal 2026
levels.body:
The US government ran a budget deficit of about $1.992 trillion in fiscal 2026, Treasury figures published on 16 October show. That is up around 12% from $1.775 trillion a year earlier and the third-largest ever, after 2020 and 2021.
Interest on the national debt, net of income, passed $1 trillion, compared with $970 billion the year before. Social Security cost nearly $1.7 trillion and Medicare almost $1.1 trillion. Individual income tax receipts exceeded $2.8 trillion, while corporate receipts fell by about $70 billion after last year's tax cuts. Customs duties were hit by refunds following a Supreme Court ruling that many tariffs were unconstitutional.
This was the 25th consecutive annual deficit, the last surplus having come in 2001.
levels.why: The cost of servicing US debt is growing, which may limit future spending and tax choices.

levels.headline: US government borrowed almost $2 trillion more than it raised this year
levels.body:
The US government spent about $1.992 trillion more than it collected in its 2026 financial year, new Treasury figures show. That is about 12% more than the $1.775 trillion gap a year earlier, and the third biggest on record after 2020 and 2021.
Paying interest on the national debt cost more than $1 trillion, up from $970 billion. Social Security cost nearly $1.7 trillion and Medicare almost $1.1 trillion. Income taxes paid by individuals raised over $2.8 trillion, but companies paid about $70 billion less after tax cuts. Money from tariffs was reduced because the Supreme Court ruled many of them unconstitutional and refunds were due.
The US has run a deficit for 25 years in a row. Its last surplus was in 2001.
levels.why: Interest on debt now takes a very large share of the US budget.

levels.headline: US deficit hits almost $2 trillion for the year
levels.body:
The US government spent nearly $2 trillion more than it received in taxes in its 2026 financial year, official figures show. The exact amount was $1.992 trillion. That is about 12% higher than last year and the third largest deficit ever.
A lot of the money went on interest. The government now pays more than $1 trillion a year in interest on its debts, up from $970 billion. Social Security, which pays pensions, cost nearly $1.7 trillion, and Medicare, which pays for health care for older people, cost almost $1.1 trillion.
Companies paid about $70 billion less in tax because of tax cuts, and money from tariffs fell because the Supreme Court ruled many were unconstitutional. The US has had a deficit for 25 years in a row.
levels.why: A big deficit means more borrowing, which can make loans costlier.

levels.headline: America spent almost $2 trillion more than it took in
levels.body:
A deficit is when a government spends more than it collects. The US government's deficit for its last financial year was about $1.992 trillion. That is around 12% more than the year before, and the third biggest ever.
One big cost was interest. The government has borrowed a lot, and each year it must pay extra on that debt. This year, interest cost more than $1 trillion. Pensions through Social Security cost nearly $1.7 trillion, and health care for older people through Medicare cost almost $1.1 trillion.
The government also collected less from company taxes because of tax cuts. Money from tariffs, which are taxes on goods from abroad, went down because the Supreme Court said many were not allowed.
levels.why: Growing debt means the government must keep paying more just to cover interest.

levels.headline: The US spent nearly $2 trillion more than it earned this year
levels.body:
Governments get money from taxes, and they spend it on things like pensions and health care. A deficit means a government spent more than it received. This year, the US government's deficit was about $1.992 trillion, which is the third biggest ever. It was about 12% bigger than last year.
To cover the gap, the government borrows money, and then it has to pay interest, which is a fee for borrowing. This year, interest cost over $1 trillion. Pensions through Social Security cost nearly $1.7 trillion. Health care for older people cost almost $1.1 trillion.
The government also got less from company taxes because of tax cuts. A court also said many tariffs, taxes on imported goods, were not allowed.
levels.why: The more a country borrows, the more it has to pay back just in interest.

levels.headline: America spent a lot more money than it collected
levels.body:
A government collects money from people and companies. It does this through taxes. Then it spends the money on things like pensions and health care. A deficit means that it spent more than it collected.
This year, the United States had a deficit of almost $2 trillion. That is a huge number. It is about 12% bigger than last year.
To fill the gap, the government borrowed money. When you borrow, you have to pay back extra, called interest. The government's interest bill is now more than $1 trillion in one year.
The government also collected less from company taxes. A court also said many taxes on goods from other countries, called tariffs, were not allowed. The United States has had a deficit for 25 years in a row.
levels.why: A big deficit means the government borrows a lot, and it has to pay it back.

levels.headline: The United States spent far more than it had
levels.body:
